misconceptions.description: Believing more cues (bold, color, boxes, arrows) always improve learning, rather than that signaling works by directing limited attention to the essential element through contrast
misconceptions.trigger: learner highlights most of the screen or stacks several cue types on one element
misconceptions.feedback: Signaling works by contrast. When everything is cued, nothing is. Cut cues until only the essential element stands out.

misconceptions.description: Treating segmenting as merely splitting text into shorter paragraphs, rather than giving the learner control over the pace of meaningful units
misconceptions.trigger: learner shortens paragraphs but keeps a single continuous auto-advancing animation
misconceptions.feedback: Segmenting gives learner-paced units, for example a continue control or a pause. Shorter paragraphs in a non-stop sequence are not segmenting.

misconceptions.description: Adding a signaling cue without checking whether the cue itself adds extraneous processing for the target learner
misconceptions.trigger: learner adds a motion or sound cue that competes with the content it is meant to highlight
misconceptions.feedback: Check the load budget. A cue that itself demands processing can cost more than the attention it saves.

misconceptions.description: Placing segment boundaries by length rather than at the seams between conceptual units
misconceptions.trigger: learner inserts a pause mid-explanation because the segment was getting long
misconceptions.feedback: Break at conceptual seams, not at arbitrary lengths. A pause inside one idea fragments the schema the learner is building.
